name: Text 5

On a hot afternoon in Tuas, a subcontractor with twenty workers pays for sixty minutes of labour and gets fifty. He is doing exactly what the rules ask. And no insurance policy in Singapore will pay him a cent for it. We are Team Chai-Kopi, and this is Rehat. In Malay it means rest. In Hindi, raahat means relief.

Call him Mr Tan. Fixed-price jobs, thin margins. Heat breaks, heavy rain and haze cost him about twelve thousand dollars a year in wages paid for work not done. The average is not what hurts. The swing is. Singapore had 37 days of high heat stress in 2023, 21 in 2024 and 29 last year. He cannot budget for that, and every policy he owns pays zero for it.

text: At a heat reading of 32, MOM requires ten minutes of rest every hour for heavy work. A work permit holder is paid his declared salary whether or not there is work. And it is enforced: MOM has acted against 213 employers. But heat is the smaller part. Two-thirds of the lost hours are heavy rain, and no boss can order the rain to stop.

name: Text 24

Rehat is one tick box on the work injury policy Mr Tan already buys from Income. Every hour we read NEA's heat, rain and haze data at his station and compare the downtime with a normal month. For every hour beyond normal we pay eight dollars per worker, before payroll. Every policy also comes with an hourly heat alert and a compliance log, which is what an MOM inspector asks to see. And we say up front: we pay on the station, not his site.

title: Downtime hours per worker, by month

text: Mr Tan already plans for heat and rain. This chart is a normal year, and a normal month is part of the job. He carries that, plus a 25 percent buffer. That is his deductible. But some months take more than their share, and those are the months a boss is tempted to skip the break. Those are the months Rehat pays. He still keeps a fifth of the cost, the limit is sixty hours a year, and normal resets yearly as the climate warms.

Rehat is profitable from the first year, with expenses budgeted at the twenty percent Income's own brief sets. Of every premium dollar, sixty-five cents go back to firms, twenty to expenses, five to reinsurance, and ten is profit: about 540,000 dollars over three years. The worst case is in the contract, 480 dollars per worker. In simulation it makes a profit seven years in ten. The loss years are El Niño years, so haze is capped and we buy stop-loss cover. And if MOM acts against a firm, its heat payout is forfeited.

Where is the AI? Not in the payout. Rules decide every dollar, so anyone can check it against NEA's data. AI sits in the interface. It reads the policy documents and quotes in minutes, explains every receipt, and turns the forecast into a warning so Mr Tan moves heavy work to the morning.

So our question to Income is simple. Would you pilot this? And if not, what would have to be true? Rest that is paid for gets taken. Thank you.
